results.text: d in my view the answer here lies not in Silicon Valley, but with a forgotten British maths professor, Wilfred Halliday Cockcroft, half a century ago. In the 1970s, the quality of maths teaching in UK schools appeared to be collapsing and numeracy was reportedly low. Cockcroft, who had a longstanding interest in mathematics education, was asked by the government to look into it. And in 1982 the Cockcroft Report was published. It was enormous, forensic – and is now largely forgotten. But it may turn out to be the most important document written for thinking about the future of education, because of its response to the electronic calculator. Related: ‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPT It is fascinating to read Cockcroft’s report and discover how the challenges of the calculator back then were so similar to the ones we face with AI today – from the fear that it would undermine “basic skills” to the intimidation many felt at the complexity of this strange new technology (“Some … had been discouraged by the large number of figures which had appeared after the decimal point”).

results.text: This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen. Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location. The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars. Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

results.text: A shark that became a viral sensation after getting stuck in a South Korean canal for a month has returned just hours after being coaxed out to sea. Nicknamed Bukang-i by fans, the 3-metre-long (9.8-foot) female dusky shark was first spotted in the waterway on 18 September. On Wednesday, workers used nets fixed to floating pontoons to guide the shark free, but it dived beneath a net and returned to the canal in Busan overnight, authorities said. “The shark is now between the outer net and an inner net installed 30 to 40 metres ... further inside the canal,” an oceans ministry official told AFP. After it got trapped in September, officials initially opted to wait for the shark to leave on its own – but amid growing concerns for its wellbeing they took a more proactive approach. A fresh attempt to free Bukang-i was under way on Thursday morning, officials said. Officials spent Thursday morning removing a screen that was potentially blocking the shark’s exit, replacing the net it had swum under and raising an outer barrier, before attempting to guide Bukang-i out again.

citation.title: Bukang-i is back: shark returns to canal in South Korea hours after being coaxed out to sea

Gradually, however, it became clear that whatever Pluto was, it wasn’t Planet X. It didn’t seem anywhere near large enough to account for irregularities in Neptune’s orbit. Eris was out in the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune – where Pluto also resides. It was roughly the same size as Pluto (less volume, but more mass). If Pluto was a planet, the argument went, then so was Eris. And if Eris wasn’t a planet, how could Pluto continue to be one? Eris and Pluto were by no means alone in the Kuiper Belt. Other smaller bodies were discovered around the same time, including Haumea, Makemake and Sedna. Were these also planets? There were likely many more similar objects still to be found. How would schoolchildren manage a planetary roster that might number in the hundreds? In search of a solution, the IAU came up with a three-point definition of a planet: it must orbit the Sun; it must have sufficient mass to pull itself into a round shape; and it must have “cleared its neighbourhood” – meaning it must gravitationally dominate the area in which it orbits. Nothing beyond Neptune that we knew about qualified; Pluto was out.

results.text: Twenty years ago, Pluto got demoted. After a vote by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, Pluto was relegated from major planet to dwarf planet status. Our solar system dropped from nine planets to eight. At the time, many scientists were unhappy with the decision. Two decades on, the debate is, if anything, even more polarised. “The definition of a planet they created, you can’t use it at all,” says Philip Metzger, the director of the Stephen W Hawking Centre for Microgravity Research and Education at the University of Central Florida. “It makes the definition of a planet completely non-useful in science.” Metzger is one of a number of scientists and lay people who consider Pluto’s demotion a big mistake. For some, Pluto’s downgraded status is the source of their affection for the ex-planet. “Pluto represents the underdog that so many people root for, the small kid on the block that is being picked on,” says Kevin Schindler, historian at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, where Pluto was discovered in 1930. For others, the IAU’s decision, and the way it was taken, is central to the debate.

The public of today is not the public of the 1800s. They’re perfectly happy understanding a dynamic, chaotic cosmos, and we missed the opportunity to teach that.” Pluto’s nature has always been elusive. Although it consists of just a handful of faint stars, Sagitta’s distinctive shape (it really does look like an arrow) makes it easy to identify against a dark sky. Sagitta can be found about partway along the imaginary line connecting Vega and Altair, which make up the summer triangle with Deneb. results.text: This week we will track down Pegasus, one of the most distinctive constellations in the autumn sky. Pegasus was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the second century. In Greek mythology, it represents the magnificent winged horse ridden by the hero Bellerophon. The easiest part of the constellation to recognise is the Great Square of Pegasus, a large pattern of four moderately bright stars. The chart shows the view looking high in the southern sky from London at 10pm on 26 October. Three of these stars, Markab, Scheat and Algenib, belong to Pegasus. The fourth, Alpheratz, is actually part of the neighbouring constellation Andromeda. Historically, Alpheratz was considered to belong to both constellations, but when the official boundaries of the 88 modern constellations were established, it ended up in Andromeda. The Great Square is the body of Pegasus. From Markab, follow a curving line of stars towards Enif (whose name means nose in Arabic) to trace the horse’s neck and head. Other lines of stars extending from the Square represent the horse’s front legs. Notice that the horse appears upside down.

results.text: We turn our attention this week to one of the sky’s smallest constellations. High overhead from the UK after darkness falls, Lyra, the lyre, is easy to find thanks to the brilliant white star of Vega. The chart shows the view facing south and looking up towards the zenith from London at 22:30 BST on 17 August. As the fifth-brightest star in the night sky, Vega forms one corner of the summer triangle, with Deneb in Cygnus, the Swan, and Altair in Aquila, the Eagle, marking the other two. Having located Vega, the rest of the constellation is easy to trace even though the stars are much fainter. One of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations, Lyra has the distinction of being a star pattern that actually looks like the figure it is named after. It represents the harp played by the Greek poet Orpheus. In Greek mythology, Orpheus played such beautiful music that he could charm wild animals, move rocks and even influence the gods. Becoming one of the Argonauts, Orpheus’s music protected the rest of the crew from the beguiling call of the Sirens.

Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen. Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location. The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars. Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

Astronomers have detected the fastest known star in the Milky Way, hurtling around the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy. The star, called S301, travels at about 25,000km (15,500 miles) per second, 100,000 times faster than a commercial plane. It is also the closest known star to the Milky Way’s central black hole, Sagittarius A*, approaching it around the distance of Saturn to the Sun. “What is special about this star is that it’s orbiting Sagittarius A* on a very tight orbit, taking just 8.7 years to complete it, and is approaching the black hole at a mere 12 times the distance of Earth to the sun. That is unprecedented,” said Felix Mang, a PhD student at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE) in Garching, Germany, and an author of the study published on the findings. The star’s extreme proximity to Sagittarius A* means that it could open a new window on to the black hole’s fundamental properties and the extreme environment surrounding it. results.text: We turn our attention this week to one of the sky’s smallest constellations. High overhead from the UK after darkness falls, Lyra, the lyre, is easy to find thanks to the brilliant white star of Vega. The chart shows the view facing south and looking up towards the zenith from London at 22:30 BST on 17 August. As the fifth-brightest star in the night sky, Vega forms one corner of the summer triangle, with Deneb in Cygnus, the Swan, and Altair in Aquila, the Eagle, marking the other two. Having located Vega, the rest of the constellation is easy to trace even though the stars are much fainter. One of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations, Lyra has the distinction of being a star pattern that actually looks like the figure it is named after. It represents the harp played by the Greek poet Orpheus. In Greek mythology, Orpheus played such beautiful music that he could charm wild animals, move rocks and even influence the gods. Becoming one of the Argonauts, Orpheus’s music protected the rest of the crew from the beguiling call of the Sirens.

results.text: This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen. Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location. The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars. Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

results.text: This week we will track down Pegasus, one of the most distinctive constellations in the autumn sky. Pegasus was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the second century. In Greek mythology, it represents the magnificent winged horse ridden by the hero Bellerophon. The easiest part of the constellation to recognise is the Great Square of Pegasus, a large pattern of four moderately bright stars. The chart shows the view looking high in the southern sky from London at 10pm on 26 October. Three of these stars, Markab, Scheat and Algenib, belong to Pegasus. The fourth, Alpheratz, is actually part of the neighbouring constellation Andromeda. Historically, Alpheratz was considered to belong to both constellations, but when the official boundaries of the 88 modern constellations were established, it ended up in Andromeda. The Great Square is the body of Pegasus. From Markab, follow a curving line of stars towards Enif (whose name means nose in Arabic) to trace the horse’s neck and head. Other lines of stars extending from the Square represent the horse’s front legs. Notice that the horse appears upside down.

results.text: To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island. This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history. A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.

results.text: High above the Dead Sea’s south-eastern shore, pilgrims once climbed to a cave they believed had sheltered Lot after he fled the destruction of Sodom. For centuries the site survived in Christian memory alone, visited by occasional pilgrims such as St Stephen the Sabaite, until the Greek archaeologist Konstantinos Politis, who has died aged 67 following a series of strokes, began excavating in 1988. He uncovered a Byzantine basilica built over the mouth of the cave, its floors still adorned with mosaics laid in the sixth and seventh centuries CE. The discovery, at Deir ’Ain ’Abata, gave physical form to one of the Bible’s most vivid stories and set the course for a career spent excavating and protecting the archaeology of Jordan’s Dead Sea shore. Dino, as Politis was widely known, excavated the Sanctuary of Lot over seven seasons between 1988 and 1996. The site had been identified by an archaeological survey in 1986 as matching a sanctuary depicted on the famous sixth-century mosaic map at Madaba in Jordan, whose location had eluded archaeologists for more than a century.

Their “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. results.text: From the garden of their Georgian townhouse in Bath in the late 18th century, a brother and sister made a series of extraordinary astronomical discoveries. A new art show in the house where the siblings – William and Caroline Herschel – worked and lived highlights their pioneering spirit and their domestic arrangements. The Irish artist Grace Weir, who created the exhibition in what is now the Herschel Museum of Astronomy, said she was deeply interested in the science that went on at the house, including the discovery of the planet Uranus, and fascinated that it took place in such a cosy environment. “It is a home,” Weir said. “Science does not take place in a vacuum. They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table.” One of her artworks, On the Construction of Heavens, was inspired by William Herschel’s drawing of the Milky Way in 1785. Weir has had a copy of the drawing embroidered on to an antique linen tablecloth, which is laid over the family dining table. “William and Caroline must have spoken about the shape of the Milky Way right here,” Weir said.

And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts. Although it is one of the brightest star clusters in the night sky, it can be surprisingly difficult to locate because Cancer contains no bright stars to guide the eye towards it. It is, of course, the annual Ig Nobel awards. Not to be confused with the more prestigious and career-changing Nobel prizes that will be announced in Scandinavia next month, the satirical Ig Nobels are awarded for achievements that “first make people laugh and then make them think”. On Thursday, real Nobel laureates were on stage to hand out the awards and winners were giving “24/7” lectures: describing their work in 24 seconds and then in seven words. Here are the 2026 winners. Economics: evil rich people Are rich people really worse behaved than the rest of us? Through a series of experiments, psychologists amassed evidence that the upper classes are indeed more prone to behaving badly, from being oblivious to other road users, lying at work and taking treats meant for children. “I’ve followed the Ig Nobels since my early college days.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000). In the 1970s, the quality of maths teaching in UK schools appeared to be collapsing and numeracy was reportedly low. Cockcroft, who had a longstanding interest in mathematics education, was asked by the government to look into it. And in 1982 the Cockcroft Report was published. It was enormous, forensic – and is now largely forgotten. But it may turn out to be the most important document written for thinking about the future of education, because of its response to the electronic calculator.

Related: ‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPT

It is fascinating to read Cockcroft’s report and discover how the challenges of the calculator back then were so similar to the ones we face with AI today – from the fear that it would undermine “basic skills” to the intimidation many felt at the complexity of this strange new technology (“Some … had been discouraged by the large number of figures which had appeared after the decimal point”).

Today’s puzzle is set by Terence Tao, who may be the world’s most famous mathematician.

Tao, aged 51, has been a global phenomenon since the age of ten, when he became the youngest competitor at the International Maths Olympiad, a record he still holds. For the last three decades he has been a professor at UCLA, where he has been garlanded with prizes, and where one of his colleagues famously said: “Terry is like Mozart: mathematics just flows out of him.”

Tao is a very visible leader of the field, not only because of his scientific contributions and collaborations, but also because he writes the most widely-read blog in research level maths. When Open AI earlier this month stunned the community with the release of hundreds of proofs of long-standing open questions – the “mathpocalypse” – his blog has become one of the most important forums for the community’s response.

This week Tao publishes Six Maths Essentials, his first work aimed at a general audience. The puzzle below reflects ideas in the book.

results.text:
This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars.

The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen.

Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location.

The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars.

Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

Jolyon Troscianko, also of the University of Exeter, said: “Butterfly wings deform as they fly, clapping together on the upstroke and peeling apart on the downstroke, so their stripes shift angle and point in different directions as they flap.

“Combined with their unpredictable flight paths, this patterning creates misleading motion illusions, causing a predator to miss entirely or to strike a less vulnerable part of the wing, such as the hindwing or tail.”

The experts compared the mechanism to the “barber pole illusion” – the red and white stripes appear to travel upwards even though the pole is only spinning in place.

The breakthrough came when Troscianko put a slow-motion video of a butterfly flying upwards through a “bird-vision” computer model. It seemed to indicate – wrongly – that the butterfly was moving downwards.

Troscianko said: “First I checked this wasn’t a coding error, that I’d swapped up and down somehow, but then it dawned on me that this would be a perfect way to confuse attacking predators.”

The team looked at hundreds of types of European butterflies and found different patterns created different effects.

This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars.

The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen.

Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location.

The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars.

Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

A shark that became a viral sensation after getting stuck in a South Korean canal for a month has returned just hours after being coaxed out to sea.

Nicknamed Bukang-i by fans, the 3-metre-long (9.8-foot) female dusky shark was first spotted in the waterway on 18 September.

On Wednesday, workers used nets fixed to floating pontoons to guide the shark free, but it dived beneath a net and returned to the canal in Busan overnight, authorities said.

“The shark is now between the outer net and an inner net installed 30 to 40 metres ... further inside the canal,” an oceans ministry official told AFP.

After it got trapped in September, officials initially opted to wait for the shark to leave on its own – but amid growing concerns for its wellbeing they took a more proactive approach. A fresh attempt to free Bukang-i was under way on Thursday morning, officials said.

Officials spent Thursday morning removing a screen that was potentially blocking the shark’s exit, replacing the net it had swum under and raising an outer barrier, before attempting to guide Bukang-i out again.

Related: The night watch: the YouTubers who are guardians of a shark stuck in a South Korean canal

results.text:
Gradually, however, it became clear that whatever Pluto was, it wasn’t Planet X. It didn’t seem anywhere near large enough to account for irregularities in Neptune’s orbit. Scientists offered theories to explain why Pluto looked so small, but the truth was, it was small – even smaller than the moon. Only in 1992 did we learn that Lowell’s calculations were based on an overestimation of Neptune’s mass. There was no Planet X.

Pluto’s reputation as an underdog, the picked-on kid, may stem from the 2006 vote, but one could argue it was punching above its weight for years. How would they have voted on Pluto’s planetary status if they had known the truth in 1930? And will it take another vote to satisfy Pluto’s defenders?

“People have locked in,” says Metzger. “We would have a less useful vote today than we did back in the 2006 timeframe. So we don’t want another vote. What we want is for people to recognise that voting was a mistake, and we’re not going to do that any more. We’re going to go back to the scientific method.”

citation.title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

results.text:
The event that sparked the IAU’s 2006 vote was the discovery of a distant celestial body that would come to be called Eris. Eris was out in the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune – where Pluto also resides. It was roughly the same size as Pluto (less volume, but more mass). If Pluto was a planet, the argument went, then so was Eris. And if Eris wasn’t a planet, how could Pluto continue to be one?

Eris and Pluto were by no means alone in the Kuiper Belt. Other smaller bodies were discovered around the same time, including Haumea, Makemake and Sedna. Were these also planets? There were likely many more similar objects still to be found. How would schoolchildren manage a planetary roster that might number in the hundreds?

In search of a solution, the IAU came up with a three-point definition of a planet: it must orbit the Sun; it must have sufficient mass to pull itself into a round shape; and it must have “cleared its neighbourhood” – meaning it must gravitationally dominate the area in which it orbits. Nothing beyond Neptune that we knew about qualified; Pluto was out.

citation.title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

results.text:
Twenty years ago, Pluto got demoted. After a vote by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, Pluto was relegated from major planet to dwarf planet status. Our solar system dropped from nine planets to eight. At the time, many scientists were unhappy with the decision. Two decades on, the debate is, if anything, even more polarised.

“The definition of a planet they created, you can’t use it at all,” says Philip Metzger, the director of the Stephen W Hawking Centre for Microgravity Research and Education at the University of Central Florida. “It makes the definition of a planet completely non-useful in science.”

Metzger is one of a number of scientists and lay people who consider Pluto’s demotion a big mistake.

For some, Pluto’s downgraded status is the source of their affection for the ex-planet. “Pluto represents the underdog that so many people root for, the small kid on the block that is being picked on,” says Kevin Schindler, historian at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, where Pluto was discovered in 1930.

citation.title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

results.text:
For Metzger, the planetary definition excluding Pluto is based on an outmoded notion of the solar system. “They were creating a reactionary view towards an orderly cosmos, rather than the more modern scientific view where it’s chaotic,” he says. “The second problem was that I think they misread the room. The public of today is not the public of the 1800s. They’re perfectly happy understanding a dynamic, chaotic cosmos, and we missed the opportunity to teach that.”

Pluto’s nature has always been elusive. In 1915, the astronomer Percival Lowell published calculations based on peculiarities in the orbits of Uranus and Neptune, predicting the existence of a new, ninth planet, which he called Planet X, with a mass somewhere between Earth’s and Neptune’s. In 1930, the long search for Planet X bore fruit: the new body, discovered at the observatory that bore Lowell’s name, was christened Pluto.

citation.title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

results.text:
For others, the IAU’s decision, and the way it was taken, is central to the debate. “My being involved with advocating for Pluto started on the day of the vote,” says writer, actor and amateur astronomer Laurel Kornfeld. “I was like: wait a minute, this is wrong.” When we meet on Zoom she is wearing a T-shirt that says: “Pluto Resistance, 20 years: 2006-2026.”

The campaign to reinstate Pluto – with its passionate advocates, ongoing debates, occasional protests and petitions – seems to be largely confined to the US. “It is more of an issue in the United States,” says Metzger. “This was the one we discovered.” So, the planet’s demotion was a source of wounded pride? “I’ll admit there was some of that – among the public, not the scientists.”

More recently, the campaign has taken on a populist tinge, with Trump’s Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, telling a congressional committee in April that he was in favour of a rethink. “I am very much in the camp of Make Pluto a Planet Again,” he said.

The event that sparked the IAU’s 2006 vote was the discovery of a distant celestial body that would come to be called Eris. Eris was out in the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune – where Pluto also resides. It was roughly the same size as Pluto (less volume, but more mass). If Pluto was a planet, the argument went, then so was Eris. And if Eris wasn’t a planet, how could Pluto continue to be one?

Eris and Pluto were by no means alone in the Kuiper Belt. Other smaller bodies were discovered around the same time, including Haumea, Makemake and Sedna. Were these also planets? There were likely many more similar objects still to be found. How would schoolchildren manage a planetary roster that might number in the hundreds?

In search of a solution, the IAU came up with a three-point definition of a planet: it must orbit the Sun; it must have sufficient mass to pull itself into a round shape; and it must have “cleared its neighbourhood” – meaning it must gravitationally dominate the area in which it orbits. Nothing beyond Neptune that we knew about qualified; Pluto was out.

Pluto’s demotion created two opposing scientific teams: the so-called geophysical camp, which believes the physical properties of a celestial body should count toward its planethood; and the dynamicists, who are more concerned with the position a body occupies, its surroundings and its direction of travel. You could characterise the split as planetary scientists v astronomers. Many planetary scientists, including Metzger, simply do not use the IAU definition.

When the New Horizons spacecraft made its flyby of Pluto in 2015, the geophysical camp seized what it saw as an advantage. Pluto definitely had the geophysical makings of a planet, they maintained. It had mountains, evidence of recent geological activity, and water ice hills floating on frozen nitrogen. It might even be able to support life. How could that not be a planet?

We are on the hunt for another small, northern summer constellation this week: Sagitta, the arrow. Although it consists of just a handful of faint stars, Sagitta’s distinctive shape (it really does look like an arrow) makes it easy to identify against a dark sky.

The chart shows the view looking up towards the zenith while facing south from London at 22.30 BST on Monday.

Sagitta can be found about partway along the imaginary line connecting Vega and Altair, which make up the summer triangle with Deneb.

Although it is the third-smallest constellation in the sky, Sagitta has been recognised since ancient times. The 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy placed it on his list of 48 constellations published in The Almagest.

There are a number of stories from Greek mythology that could be attributed to the arrow. It could be the one fired by Hercules to kill the eagle tormenting Prometheus, or it could be one of Cupid’s famous arrows.

Observers in the southern hemisphere can also see Sagitta during August, although it appears lower in the northern sky than it does from the UK.

This week we will track down Pegasus, one of the most distinctive constellations in the autumn sky. Pegasus was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the second century. In Greek mythology, it represents the magnificent winged horse ridden by the hero Bellerophon.

The easiest part of the constellation to recognise is the Great Square of Pegasus, a large pattern of four moderately bright stars. The chart shows the view looking high in the southern sky from London at 10pm on 26 October.

Three of these stars, Markab, Scheat and Algenib, belong to Pegasus. The fourth, Alpheratz, is actually part of the neighbouring constellation Andromeda. Historically, Alpheratz was considered to belong to both constellations, but when the official boundaries of the 88 modern constellations were established, it ended up in Andromeda.

The Great Square is the body of Pegasus. From Markab, follow a curving line of stars towards Enif (whose name means nose in Arabic) to trace the horse’s neck and head. Other lines of stars extending from the Square represent the horse’s front legs. Notice that the horse appears upside down.

The observations were made using the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope Interferometer (ESO’s VLTI) at the Paranal Observatory in Chile, which combines the light from four 8-metre telescopes.

Although the star is unusually close to the central black hole, it is not expected to cross its event horizon, the point beyond which objects can never escape.

“Black holes are perceived as these cosmic vacuum cleaners engulfing everything they can get a handle on,” said Mang. “But it’s just a massive object. It’s not really much different from something orbiting the sun and it’s going to remain on this orbit.”

Dr Ziri Younsi, an astrophysicist at University College London, who was not involved in the observations, said: “This is incredibly important as a discovery. It’s very exciting because this thing comes insanely close to Sagittarius A* and it’s travelling, at its peak, at about 8% of the speed of light, which is crazy.”

Younsi said that using the orbit to provide a measurement of the black hole’s spin would be a gamechanger for understanding the evolution of the Milky Way.

This week offers an excellent opportunity to track down Saturn. The giant planet, situated about 10 times further from the sun than the Earth, reached opposition on 4 October. In this configuration, Earth is passing almost directly between the planet and the sun.

This makes opposition an excellent time to see a planet: the distant world rises as the sun sets, remains visible throughout the night and sets around sunrise. It is also at about its closest point to Earth for the year.

Saturn is easily visible to the naked eye, looking like a moderately bright, creamy-white object. Unlike most stars, however, its light remains steady rather than noticeably twinkling.

The chart shows the view looking east- south-east from London at 2100 BST on 5 October. By this time, Saturn is already well clear of the horizon and will continue climbing higher as the evening progresses. It lies beneath the Great Square of Pegasus, which provides a distinctive signpost to the planet.

Although the planet itself is an easy naked-eye target, you will need a small telescope to see its famous rings. From the southern hemisphere, Saturn is even better placed, climbing higher into the sky.

Forced emojis don’t always work. That one has probably endured, says Aleksic, because “there is something intuitive about it. But the way we communicate is changing so quickly that emojis in general might be losing their appeal among young people, says Aleksic. “Stickers are becoming more popular overall,” he says, predicting that “there could be a shift away from these preset icons that the apps hand you, and more toward reaction images”.

We are on the hunt for another small, northern summer constellation this week: Sagitta, the arrow. Although it consists of just a handful of faint stars, Sagitta’s distinctive shape (it really does look like an arrow) makes it easy to identify against a dark sky.

The chart shows the view looking up towards the zenith while facing south from London at 22.30 BST on Monday.

Sagitta can be found about partway along the imaginary line connecting Vega and Altair, which make up the summer triangle with Deneb.

Although it is the third-smallest constellation in the sky, Sagitta has been recognised since ancient times. The 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy placed it on his list of 48 constellations published in The Almagest.

There are a number of stories from Greek mythology that could be attributed to the arrow. It could be the one fired by Hercules to kill the eagle tormenting Prometheus, or it could be one of Cupid’s famous arrows.

Observers in the southern hemisphere can also see Sagitta during August, although it appears lower in the northern sky than it does from the UK.

We turn our attention this week to one of the sky’s smallest constellations. High overhead from the UK after darkness falls, Lyra, the lyre, is easy to find thanks to the brilliant white star of Vega.

The chart shows the view facing south and looking up towards the zenith from London at 22:30 BST on 17 August.

As the fifth-brightest star in the night sky, Vega forms one corner of the summer triangle, with Deneb in Cygnus, the Swan, and Altair in Aquila, the Eagle, marking the other two.

Having located Vega, the rest of the constellation is easy to trace even though the stars are much fainter. One of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations, Lyra has the distinction of being a star pattern that actually looks like the figure it is named after. It represents the harp played by the Greek poet Orpheus.

In Greek mythology, Orpheus played such beautiful music that he could charm wild animals, move rocks and even influence the gods. Becoming one of the Argonauts, Orpheus’s music protected the rest of the crew from the beguiling call of the Sirens.

results.text:
To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island.

This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history.

A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.

results.text:
While professional archaeologists often worked with local people, Noble said, “it’s not always the community themselves coming up with the ideas. Here, it was very much a bottom-up approach of the heritage society coming up with a plan, working with professionals – and lo and behold, what a great series of discoveries they’ve made at the site.”

Hay said he hoped the finds would go some way to restoring the reputation of Moluag, who has long been overshadowed by the more celebrated Saint Columba, the founder of Iona and the subject of an influential ninth-century biography. “Unfortunately, Moluag never had a hagiographer, so his contribution to the evangelisation of Scotland has been very much underestimated,” he said. “So finding his monastic site and [the evidence of metalworking] – it’s all about recalibrating the situation. I think Moluag had a very big impact on the evangelising of Scotland, but unfortunately, he didn’t get his PR right.”

The results of the community excavations will be published in the forthcoming edition of Antiquity.

High above the Dead Sea’s south-eastern shore, pilgrims once climbed to a cave they believed had sheltered Lot after he fled the destruction of Sodom. For centuries the site survived in Christian memory alone, visited by occasional pilgrims such as St Stephen the Sabaite, until the Greek archaeologist Konstantinos Politis, who has died aged 67 following a series of strokes, began excavating in 1988.

He uncovered a Byzantine basilica built over the mouth of the cave, its floors still adorned with mosaics laid in the sixth and seventh centuries CE. The discovery, at Deir ’Ain ’Abata, gave physical form to one of the Bible’s most vivid stories and set the course for a career spent excavating and protecting the archaeology of Jordan’s Dead Sea shore.

Dino, as Politis was widely known, excavated the Sanctuary of Lot over seven seasons between 1988 and 1996. The site had been identified by an archaeological survey in 1986 as matching a sanctuary depicted on the famous sixth-century mosaic map at Madaba in Jordan, whose location had eluded archaeologists for more than a century.

results.text:
Their “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west.

In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded by Saint Mo Luóc or Moluag, was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say.

To Robert Hay, a retired plant scientist who moved to the island in 2001 and who coordinated the fundraising and volunteer efforts, the experience was thrilling. “We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area. To be digging out the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland – it’s extraordinary,” he said.

From the garden of their Georgian townhouse in Bath in the late 18th century, a brother and sister made a series of extraordinary astronomical discoveries.

A new art show in the house where the siblings – William and Caroline Herschel – worked and lived highlights their pioneering spirit and their domestic arrangements.

The Irish artist Grace Weir, who created the exhibition in what is now the Herschel Museum of Astronomy, said she was deeply interested in the science that went on at the house, including the discovery of the planet Uranus, and fascinated that it took place in such a cosy environment.

“It is a home,” Weir said. “Science does not take place in a vacuum. They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table.”

One of her artworks, On the Construction of Heavens, was inspired by William Herschel’s drawing of the Milky Way in 1785.

Weir has had a copy of the drawing embroidered on to an antique linen tablecloth, which is laid over the family dining table. “William and Caroline must have spoken about the shape of the Milky Way right here,” Weir said. “That would have been an unusual thing to talk about back then.”

citation.title: Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers

The accelerating retreat of European glaciers, which scientists say is primarily driven by human-caused global heating, has revealed a vast array of relics, ancient ecosystems and human remains in recent decades.

In 2015, a barracks where Italian troops had sheltered while fighting the Austro-Hungarian army during the White war – a battle waged across Alpine terrain during the first world war – was discovered on Mount Scorluzzo, a peak overlooking the Stelvio pass. The bodies of dozens of soldiers, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice in the past 20 years.

The most extraordinary discovery of human remains on a melting glacier was made in 1991 when two German hikers found the 5,300-year-old mummified body of a hunter in the Ötztal Alps, close to Italy’s border with Austria. The body of “Ötzi the Iceman”, replete with tattoos, is on display at a museum in Bolzano.

The team behind the CosmoCube mission, which is expected to last two years, said taking observations from the far side of the moon should avoid many of the challenges faced by Earth-based instruments.

“The total cost is estimated to be just under £50m and the launching date – we expect it to be about five years from now,” said de Lera Acedo, adding that CosmoCube had already been granted more than £2m of funding by the UK Space Agency.

Phil Bull, a professor of cosmology at the Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics who is not involved in the project, welcomed the mission.

“The CosmoCube measurements will help us understand the major ingredients of our cosmic origins – the processes that led to the formation of the first stars and galaxies, and lit up the Universe after a period called the cosmic dark ages,” he said.

But, Bull noted, CosmoCube was not the only mission trying to make these measurements, and others may get there first.

results.text:
Humans have a cognitive quirk for the number three. Think of the many stories that use it, from The Three Little Pigs to Goldilocks and the Three Bears and The Three Musketeers. Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity.

Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts.

citation.title: Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

results.text:
So, what is it about MacLean’s model that we just can’t seem to let go of? Well, as we’ve seen, people really do seem to love threes. But perhaps there’s more to it than that. The triune brain tells us an ego-stroking story about our place in the world: that we really are the pinnacle of evolution, standing apart from other species. It reaffirms heady ideas about our sovereignty over nature, and tells a reassuring story about our logical, orderly, almost computational abilities. We are storytelling creatures, of course, but this is a story that needs updating – to one about how much in common we have with other animals, and how simplistic assumptions about the way our minds work are almost never true.

results.text:
Human behaviour was thought to be a result of interactions between all three layers of the triune brain. Frayed tempers, impulsive acts and short termism were signs of the lizard brain winning out. The notion of reptilian impulses “breaking through” proved so popular it found its way into the worlds of pop psychology, business and self-help, and has proved remarkably tenacious. A mini-industry of books, talks and training grew up around the idea that you could draw on the power of the neomammalian brain to keep basic, unhelpful or destructive emotions in check.

The underpinning analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists. It’s easy to grasp, sure, and tells a compelling story. But evolution just doesn’t bolt-on neatly divisible mental capacities in this way.

As Guy Leschziner, consultant neurologist at London’s Guy’s and St Thomas’ hospital put it to me: “the concept of different parts of the brain having different functions is extremely well established. However, to portray humans as having different brain layers, for example a ‘lizard brain’ underlying basic physiological functions, is not borne out by evolutionary or physiological evidence. results.text:
Deep inside, at the centre, lurks the primitive lizard brain, retained from an ancestor we share with reptiles. This contains ancient regions responsible for survival, helping us to hunt and forage, and driving our sexual impulses so that we reproduce. A second layer sits wrapped around the first, the so-called mammalian brain. It contains the limbic system, deemed to be the seat of our emotions. It enabled mammals to play, care for and nurse their young and communicate in some crude way.

The third and final layer, sheathing all of this and making humans in particular a cut above, is the “neomammalian” brain: the eminently rational cortex. This, it was proposed, provides us with our superior intellect, capacity for language and ability to reason. According to MacLean, it helped to keep in check our primitive, lizard-like impulses and rudimentary emotional reactions.

The analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists

This week offers an excellent opportunity to track down Saturn. The giant planet, situated about 10 times further from the sun than the Earth, reached opposition on 4 October. In this configuration, Earth is passing almost directly between the planet and the sun.

This makes opposition an excellent time to see a planet: the distant world rises as the sun sets, remains visible throughout the night and sets around sunrise. It is also at about its closest point to Earth for the year.

Saturn is easily visible to the naked eye, looking like a moderately bright, creamy-white object. Unlike most stars, however, its light remains steady rather than noticeably twinkling.

The chart shows the view looking east- south-east from London at 2100 BST on 5 October. By this time, Saturn is already well clear of the horizon and will continue climbing higher as the evening progresses. It lies beneath the Great Square of Pegasus, which provides a distinctive signpost to the planet.

This week offers one of the better opportunities of the year to catch a glimpse of the solar system’s innermost world. Trapped in its small orbit, Mercury never strays far from the sun, meaning it is usually lost to the light of dawn or dusk. On Sunday, however, the planet reached its greatest western elongation, meaning it appeared at its greatest apparent distance from the sun in the morning sky.

The next few mornings offer one of the best opportunities this year for catching a glimpse of the planet as it steadily brightens, improving the contrast with the gathering dawn. An early start and an unobstructed view towards the east-north-east will be essential to making the sighting. The chart shows the view looking in this direction from London at 04.30 BST on Tuesday.

If your line of sight is free from obstructions, the planet will become visible about a handspan above the horizon some time between 04.30 and 05.00. Binoculars can help, but exercise caution: sunrise on Tuesday from London occurs at 05.28, so stop using binoculars well before this time to protect your eyesight.

As a bonus, Mars will be much easier to spot, higher and to the east.

In the basement workshop, where William Herschel built his own telescopes, Weir has installed an LED digital counter that records the distance of Uranus from the Earth as it changes.

A key element of the show is to make sure Caroline Herschel gets her share of the credit for the pair’s advances in science.

One of the most striking pieces Weir has created is a tribute to Caroline Herschel’s comet-spotting abilities. Called An Imperfect Account, it features a piece of meteorite and a piece of obsidian in the shape of one of Caroline’s worry beads.

The September or autumnal equinox takes place this week. It marks the astronomical beginning of autumn in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere. This year, the precise moment of the equinox falls at 01.05 BST on 23 September.

It is commonly said the equinox is when day and night are equal, because the name derives from the Latin for “equal night”, but in practice that is not quite true. An equinox occurs when the sun crosses the celestial equator, the imaginary projection of Earth’s equator into the sky.

As Earth moves around its orbit, the sun’s apparent position shifts north and south of the celestial equator. At the equinox it crosses from one side to the other. But even then, day and night are not precisely equal.

This is because the sun appears as a disc rather than a point of light, and the bending of its rays by our atmosphere means we can still see it even when it is just below the horizon. Together, these effects make the measured daytime several minutes longer than 12 hours at the equinox.

This week offers one of the better opportunities of the year to catch a glimpse of the solar system’s innermost world. Trapped in its small orbit, Mercury never strays far from the sun, meaning it is usually lost to the light of dawn or dusk. On Sunday, however, the planet reached its greatest western elongation, meaning it appeared at its greatest apparent distance from the sun in the morning sky.

The next few mornings offer one of the best opportunities this year for catching a glimpse of the planet as it steadily brightens, improving the contrast with the gathering dawn. Binoculars can help, but exercise caution: sunrise on Tuesday from London occurs at 05.28, so stop using binoculars well before this time to protect your eyesight.

As a bonus, Mars will be much easier to spot, higher and to the east.

The Nobel prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has been awarded to three scientists for their work investigating the mysteries of the brain.

Karl Deisseroth of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg have been awarded the prize “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”.

The Nobel assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, announced the winners on Monday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).

The 2026 award is the 117th time the prize has been given. Of the 235 laureates – including the latest winners – only 14 have been women and none have been awarded to black scientists.

In a nutshell the trio’s research led to the development of a light-sensitive switch that can be used to control nerve cells in the living brain, switching them on or off.

Jonathan Levin, the president of Stanford University, said the subsequent discoveries by Deisseroth, along with those of his fellow laureates, have deepened understanding of neural circuits and how they shape feelings, behaviour, and more.

“Their implications are profound, not only for understanding the human brain, but for opening possibilities into new treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders,” he said.

The work had its origins in research by Hegemann, who wanted to explore how a green alga called Chlamydomonas swam towards light. “He discovered that its eye spot contains a light-sensitive protein that converts light almost instantly into an electrical signal, allowing the alga to move,” said Abdel El Manira, a professor of neuroscience at the Karolinska Institute and member of the Nobel assembly.

Nagel and Hegemann identified the proteins, called channelrhodopsins, and working with frog egg cells they revealed that when the proteins were exposed to blue light, they allowed charged particles – or ions – to flow into the cell, producing an electrical impulse.

The Nobel prize in physics 2026 has been awarded to a researcher who turned an enormous block of ice at the south pole into a detector for ghostly particles called neutrinos that reach Earth from outer space.

Prof Francis Halzen, a Belgian particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, led work on the IceCube neutrino observatory, which made the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, soon after it was switched on.

To build the observatory, scientists, technicians and engineers embedded thousands of basketball-sized light detectors into a cubic kilometre of ice to detect faint flashes of light that can result when neutrinos from space crash into atomic nuclei.

Announcing the prize on Tuesday, the Nobel committee said Halzen won “for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. He receives a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).

Starwatch: Tracking down the faint stars of Pisces

This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen. Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location. The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars. Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

“European governments must create conditions that attract investment in next-generation medicines before it’s too late,” said the letter, which was also signed by the chairs of Germany’s Boehringer Ingelheim, Italy’s Chiesi group, France’s Sanofi and Ipsen, and Novartis and Roche of Switzerland. Europe’s share of global pharmaceutical research and development has fallen from 43% in 1990 to 31%, according to the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA). The continent’s share of commercial clinical trials – where new medicines are tested for safety and efficacy before they are submitted for regulatory approval – has halved to 9% from 18% a decade ago. Only 4% of clinical trials are focused on cell and gene therapies. China has overtaken Europe in clinical trials, pharmaceutical patents, and the development of new medicines. “Sometimes books tell you more than the content,” says Tim White, as he lines up carefully dust-jacketed books and pamphlets in plastic sleeves on temporary shelves in Melbourne University’s Wilson Hall. For people like White, who runs independent bookshop Books for Cooks, the book as a physical object is just as important as what’s inside it. “We’re interested in where food and society connect … So we just keep pushing the boundaries, looking for things that show unusual aspects of that, things that tell us a bit more about what it is to be human,” he says. “That’s what most of us [rare booksellers] do. We handle things that have a story.” But vendors and rare books experts are increasingly worried that these artefacts may be under threat of destruction by generative AI companies seeking to feed their ravenous technology with new texts. Secondhand booksellers in UK and Ireland suspect AI firms behind ‘strange’ bulk orders

Secondhand booksellers in the UK and Ireland are reporting a flurry of bulk orders from mystery buyers, amid speculation AI companies are acquiring the tomes for their data. Bookshops contacted by the Guardian say they have been receiving orders from buyers in the US, Canada, continental Europe and the UK. The increase has been replicated around the world, with booksellers in the US, Australia and Europe also reporting unusual orders. Stuart Manley, the co-owner of Barter Books in Alnwick, Northumberland, said the orders, which began arriving three months ago, were unusual because they did not follow the typical pattern of being grouped into themes such as sport or motoring. “It’s definitely a strange combination of books,” said Manley. “Normally a book order is on a theme but this is all over the place.” A recent order included requests for an Estonian translation of John le Carré’s The Mission Song, a copy of Anne Brontë’s Agnes Grey from a specific imprint and the October 1983 edition of Warship, a monthly magazine.

Starwatch: Sagitta’s arrow shape makes it easy to see against a dark sky

We are on the hunt for another small, northern summer constellation this week: Sagitta, the arrow. Although it consists of just a handful of faint stars, Sagitta’s distinctive shape (it really does look like an arrow) makes it easy to identify against a dark sky. The chart shows the view looking up towards the zenith while facing south from London at 22.30 BST on Monday. Sagitta can be found about partway along the imaginary line connecting Vega and Altair, which make up the summer triangle with Deneb. Although it is the third-smallest constellation in the sky, Sagitta has been recognised since ancient times. The 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy placed it on his list of 48 constellations published in The Almagest. There are a number of stories from Greek mythology that could be attributed to the arrow. It could be the one fired by Hercules to kill the eagle tormenting Prometheus, or it could be one of Cupid’s famous arrows. Observers in the southern hemisphere can also see Sagitta during August, although it appears lower in the northern sky than it does from the UK.

citation.title: Starwatch: Sagitta’s arrow shape makes it easy to see against a dark sky

Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way

Astronomers have detected the fastest known star in the Milky Way, hurtling around the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy. The star, called S301, travels at about 25,000km (15,500 miles) per second, 100,000 times faster than a commercial plane. It is also the closest known star to the Milky Way’s central black hole, Sagittarius A*, approaching it around the distance of Saturn to the Sun. “What is special about this star is that it’s orbiting Sagittarius A* on a very tight orbit, taking just 8.7 years to complete it, and is approaching the black hole at a mere 12 times the distance of Earth to the sun. That is unprecedented,” said Felix Mang, a PhD student at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE) in Garching, Germany, and an author of the study published on the findings. The star’s extreme proximity to Sagittarius A* means that it could open a new window on to the black hole’s fundamental properties and the extreme environment surrounding it. Like many objects in the night sky, black holes are predicted to spin.

citation.title: Astronomers detect fastest known star in Milky Way

Starwatch: Bright stars of Pegasus make this distinctive constellation easy to see

This week we will track down Pegasus, one of the most distinctive constellations in the autumn sky. Pegasus was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the second century. In Greek mythology, it represents the magnificent winged horse ridden by the hero Bellerophon. The easiest part of the constellation to recognise is the Great Square of Pegasus, a large pattern of four moderately bright stars. The chart shows the view looking high in the southern sky from London at 10pm on 26 October. Three of these stars, Markab, Scheat and Algenib, belong to Pegasus. The fourth, Alpheratz, is actually part of the neighbouring constellation Andromeda. Historically, Alpheratz was considered to belong to both constellations, but when the official boundaries of the 88 modern constellations were established, it ended up in Andromeda. The Great Square is the body of Pegasus. From Markab, follow a curving line of stars towards Enif (whose name means nose in Arabic) to trace the horse’s neck and head. Other lines of stars extending from the Square represent the horse’s front legs.

citation.title: Starwatch: Bright stars of Pegasus make this distinctive constellation easy to see

Starwatch: Bright stars of Pegasus make this distinctive constellation easy to see

This week we will track down Pegasus, one of the most distinctive constellations in the autumn sky. Pegasus was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the second century. In Greek mythology, it represents the magnificent winged horse ridden by the hero Bellerophon. The easiest part of the constellation to recognise is the Great Square of Pegasus, a large pattern of four moderately bright stars. The chart shows the view looking high in the southern sky from London at 10pm on 26 October. Three of these stars, Markab, Scheat and Algenib, belong to Pegasus. The fourth, Alpheratz, is actually part of the neighbouring constellation Andromeda. Historically, Alpheratz was considered to belong to both constellations, but when the official boundaries of the 88 modern constellations were established, it ended up in Andromeda. The Great Square is the body of Pegasus. From Markab, follow a curving line of stars towards Enif (whose name means nose in Arabic) to trace the horse’s neck and head. Other lines of stars extending from the Square represent the horse’s front legs.

Starwatch: Tracking down the faint stars of Pisces

This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen. Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location. The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars. Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

We turn our attention this week to one of the sky’s smallest constellations. High overhead from the UK after darkness falls, Lyra, the lyre, is easy to find thanks to the brilliant white star of Vega. The chart shows the view facing south and looking up towards the zenith from London at 22:30 BST on 17 August. As the fifth-brightest star in the night sky, Vega forms one corner of the summer triangle, with Deneb in Cygnus, the Swan, and Altair in Aquila, the Eagle, marking the other two. Having located Vega, the rest of the constellation is easy to trace even though the stars are much fainter. One of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations, Lyra has the distinction of being a star pattern that actually looks like the figure it is named after. It represents the harp played by the Greek poet Orpheus. In Greek mythology, Orpheus played such beautiful music that he could charm wild animals, move rocks and even influence the gods. Becoming one of the Argonauts, Orpheus’s music protected the rest of the crew from the beguiling call of the Sirens.

To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island. This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history. A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.

Hiker reunited with backpack 60 years after he fell into a glacier in Austria

The accelerating retreat of European glaciers, which scientists say is primarily driven by human-caused global heating, has revealed a vast array of relics, ancient ecosystems and human remains in recent decades. In 2015, a barracks where Italian troops had sheltered while fighting the Austro-Hungarian army during the White war – a battle waged across Alpine terrain during the first world war – was discovered on Mount Scorluzzo, a peak overlooking the Stelvio pass. The bodies of dozens of soldiers, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice in the past 20 years. The most extraordinary discovery of human remains on a melting glacier was made in 1991 when two German hikers found the 5,300-year-old mummified body of a hunter in the Ötztal Alps, close to Italy’s border with Austria. The body of “Ötzi the Iceman”, replete with tattoos, is on display at a museum in Bolzano.

Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

Humans have a cognitive quirk for the number three. Think of the many stories that use it, from The Three Little Pigs to Goldilocks and the Three Bears and The Three Musketeers. Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity. Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts. Deep inside, at the centre, lurks the primitive lizard brain, retained from an ancestor we share with reptiles.

Yet despite the mounting evidence, and the success of more recent frameworks, the triune brain endures. Anna Wedell, a professor at Karolinska Institute and a member of the Nobel committee for physiology or medicine, said the laureates’ work had provided new possibilities to map which cells were responsible for which functions, and which cells communicated with each other, opening up a new understanding of the function of the brain. “We’ve had anatomical maps and correlations, but now we have a tool that can provide cause-and-effect relationships so we can get a functional map of the brain, exactly pinpoint which cells do what, which cells are responsible for creating behaviours or even emotions and memories in the brain,” she said. Wedell said that by studying animals to understand how a normal, healthy brain worked, it was then possible to explore what happened when thing went wrong – for example in the case of diseases such as dementia, epilepsy and addiction. “By understanding which cells are active in these diseases in the mouse, we can also understand where to look in the human,” she said.

Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

The notion of reptilian impulses “breaking through” proved so popular it found its way into the worlds of pop psychology, business and self-help, and has proved remarkably tenacious. A mini-industry of books, talks and training grew up around the idea that you could draw on the power of the neomammalian brain to keep basic, unhelpful or destructive emotions in check. The underpinning analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists. It’s easy to grasp, sure, and tells a compelling story. But evolution just doesn’t bolt-on neatly divisible mental capacities in this way. MacLean conducted dissections of living creatures to try to prove his theory, but the results, and his interpretations of them, have since been largely discredited. For example, it’s now accepted that many reptiles do actually possess the “mammalian” limbic system, while all mammals exhibit “neomammalian” features previously thought to be unique to “higher” ones like us.

Well, as we’ve seen, people really do seem to love threes. But perhaps there’s more to it than that. The triune brain tells us an ego-stroking story about our place in the world: that we really are the pinnacle of evolution, standing apart from other species. It reaffirms heady ideas about our sovereignty over nature, and tells a reassuring story about our logical, orderly, almost computational abilities. We are storytelling creatures, of course, but this is a story that needs updating – to one about how much in common we have with other animals, and how simplistic assumptions about the way our minds work are almost never true. • Dr Hannah Critchlow is a neuroscientist and author of The 21st Century Brain (Torva). Starwatch: how to spot Saturn as it makes it closest approach to Earth this year

This week offers an excellent opportunity to track down Saturn. The giant planet, situated about 10 times further from the sun than the Earth, reached opposition on 4 October. In this configuration, Earth is passing almost directly between the planet and the sun. This makes opposition an excellent time to see a planet: the distant world rises as the sun sets, remains visible throughout the night and sets around sunrise. It is also at about its closest point to Earth for the year. Saturn is easily visible to the naked eye, looking like a moderately bright, creamy-white object. Unlike most stars, however, its light remains steady rather than noticeably twinkling. The chart shows the view looking east- south-east from London at 2100 BST on 5 October. By this time, Saturn is already well clear of the horizon and will continue climbing higher as the evening progresses. It lies beneath the Great Square of Pegasus, which provides a distinctive signpost to the planet. Saturn is currently shining at about magnitude +0.3. Once you have identified it, try returning to it on subsequent evenings.

This week offers one of the better opportunities of the year to catch a glimpse of the solar system’s innermost world. Trapped in its small orbit, Mercury never strays far from the sun, meaning it is usually lost to the light of dawn or dusk. On Sunday, however, the planet reached its greatest western elongation, meaning it appeared at its greatest apparent distance from the sun in the morning sky. The next few mornings offer one of the best opportunities this year for catching a glimpse of the planet as it steadily brightens, improving the contrast with the gathering dawn. An early start and an unobstructed view towards the east-north-east will be essential to making the sighting. The chart shows the view looking in this direction from London at 04.30 BST on Tuesday. If your line of sight is free from obstructions, the planet will become visible about a handspan above the horizon some time between 04.30 and 05.00. Binoculars can help, but exercise caution: sunrise on Tuesday from London occurs at 05.28, so stop using binoculars well before this time to protect your eyesight.

The humble one-celled alga that helped scientists win the Nobel prize

A tiny alga has helped show how memories, feelings and behaviour form in our brains, in research by three scientists awarded the Nobel prize for physiology or medicine this month. Chlamydomonas is a one-celled alga that swims towards light using a light-sensing protein called channelrhodopsin, remarkably similar to the rhodopsin in our eyes. When the channelrhodopsin detects light, electrically charged ions rush into the cell from outside, triggering an electrical signal incredibly fast that tells the alga to move with its hair-like motor. In the research, the gene for the Chlamydomonas channelrhodopsin was transferred into living animal brain cells and flashes of light were used to switch individual neurons on or off, helping pinpoint the exact circuits in the brain that control behaviour, feelings, memories, movements, waking and sleeping, and other bodily functions. It could even switch on how mice gather their young in a nest or groom them.
